messages.ui.rootsTitle: Learning science and valuing our languages.
messages.ui.rootsDescription: We share astronomy explanations and words for the sky. Community knowledge is included through the voices of its speakers.
messages.ui.observeDescription: You do not need a telescope to begin. Share a moment under the stars with your family or community, and keep a notebook of discoveries.
messages.ui.step1: Find a safe place with little artificial light and a clear sky. Bring warm clothing and company.
messages.ui.step2: Let your eyes adjust to the dark for about 20 minutes. Avoid looking at your screen.
messages.ui.step3: Draw what you see. Record the time, place, and words your family uses to name the sky.
messages.ui.footer: Connecting Earth and sky. Puno, Peru.

messages.article.stars.title: Stars and galaxies
messages.article.stars.p1: Stars are huge spheres of hot gas that produce energy inside them. Our Sun is one of them. Light from other stars travels for years before reaching our eyes: looking into space also means looking into the past.
messages.article.stars.p2: Stars gather in galaxies. We live in the Milky Way, home to billions of stars. On a dark night, part of it appears as a faint band across the sky.
messages.article.stars.p3: Nebulae are clouds of gas and dust. Some form new stars; others contain material released by dying stars. Telescope photographs show details and colors that our eyes cannot always distinguish.
messages.article.stars.summary: Learn about stars, galaxies, and clouds of gas in space.
messages.article.planets.title: The solar system
messages.article.planets.p1: The solar system consists of the Sun and the bodies orbiting it. The Sun is a star; planets shine mainly by reflecting its light.
messages.article.planets.p2: Moving outward from the Sun, the eight planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. The first four are rocky planets. Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants; Uranus and Neptune are ice giants.
messages.article.planets.p3: Saturn’s rings contain countless pieces of ice and rock. They may look solid in illustrations, but they consist of particles of different sizes.
messages.article.planets.p4: There are also moons, asteroids, comets, and dwarf planets such as Pluto. Our Moon reflects sunlight. Its phases change with the relative positions of Earth, the Moon, and the Sun.
messages.article.planets.summary: Discover the Sun, the eight planets, and other solar system bodies.
messages.article.andes.title: Languages and the sky
messages.article.andes.p1: Inti and Willka are words associated with the Sun in Quechua and Aymara. Killa and Phaxsi name the Moon; Qoyllur and Wara wara name stars. Spellings and usage may vary across communities.
messages.article.andes.p2: QAS brings astronomy and Indigenous languages together. There is no single Andean perspective: communities have their own voices, experiences, and ways of sharing knowledge.
messages.article.andes.p4: This version includes articles in four languages. The Quechua and Aymara translations are drafts generated with AI assistance. They still need review and adaptation by community speakers.
messages.article.andes.summary: Discover words for the sky and a way to learn with your community.
messages.article.mission.title: One shared sky. Many voices.
messages.article.mission.p1: QAS — Quechua Aimara Space — is an educational project bringing space closer to communities in Puno and across Peru. It is for students, families, and curious people of all ages.
messages.article.mission.p2: Explore astronomy, discover vocabulary, and download a guide to observing the sky without a telescope.
messages.article.mission.p3: You can read the articles in Spanish, English, Quechua, and Aymara. The Quechua and Aymara versions are initial translations. Review with local speakers and adaptation to their language varieties are still pending.
messages.article.sources.title: Sources and languages
messages.article.sources.p1: Astronomy concepts include links to NASA educational resources. Vocabulary draws on materials from Peru’s Reniec and Ministry of Education.
messages.article.sources.p2: Quechua and Aymara have their own varieties and contexts. The translations are drafts generated with AI assistance and have not yet been validated by local speakers. Proper names are preserved. Scientific terms are accompanied by simple explanations.
messages.article.sources.p3: The mountain photograph is illustrative and is not identified as a photograph of Puno. Photography: Unsplash. Topic symbols and the constellation are illustrations; they do not represent a current observation.
messages.article.sun.title: The Sun: our star
messages.article.sun.p1: The Sun is the closest star to Earth. Its light and heat provide many of the conditions that life on our planet needs.
messages.article.sun.p2: The Sun is made mostly of hydrogen and helium. In its core, nuclear fusion turns hydrogen into helium and releases energy. It is not a bonfire: its energy is produced in a different way.
messages.article.sun.p3: Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach Earth. This light also illuminates the Moon and the planets.
messages.article.sun.p4: Never look directly at the Sun. Ordinary sunglasses do not protect your eyes for solar viewing. This activity involves looking at shadows without looking toward the Sun.
messages.article.sun.summary: Learn where the Sun’s light and heat come from.
messages.article.sun.activity: Place an object on the ground in a safe location. Draw its shadow in the morning and afternoon. Record the time and compare the direction and size of the shadows.
messages.article.moon.title: The Moon and its phases
messages.article.moon.p1: The Moon is Earth’s natural satellite. A natural satellite is a body that travels around a planet. The Moon reflects sunlight.
messages.article.moon.p2: Half of the Moon receives sunlight. From Earth, we see different portions of that illuminated half. This makes the Moon appear to change shape. These changes are called phases.
messages.article.moon.p3: At new moon, the illuminated side faces mainly away from Earth. At full moon, we see almost all of that illuminated side. Waxing and waning phases occur between them. The cycle lasts about 29 and a half days.
messages.article.moon.p4: Earth’s shadow does not cause the phases. Earth’s shadow can darken the Moon during a lunar eclipse. The Moon can also be visible during the day, depending on its phase and position.
messages.article.moon.summary: Understand why the Moon appears to change shape.
messages.article.moon.activity: Observe the Moon for a week whenever it is visible. Draw its illuminated part and record the date and time. If you cannot see it, note whether clouds or buildings blocked that direction.
messages.article.earth.title: Earth, day, and the seasons
messages.article.earth.p1: Earth is the planet where we live. It has an atmosphere, a layer of gases surrounding the planet, and liquid water on its surface.
messages.article.earth.p2: Earth spins on its axis. This motion is called rotation and takes about 24 hours. The side facing the Sun has daytime. The opposite side has nighttime.
messages.article.earth.p3: Earth also moves around the Sun. One complete orbit takes about one year. This motion is called revolution.
messages.article.earth.p4: Earth’s axis is tilted. This tilt changes how much light each hemisphere receives during the year and causes the seasons. The seasons are not mainly caused by the distance from the Sun.
messages.article.earth.p5: Puno is in the Southern Hemisphere. Changes in rainfall and temperature also depend on a community’s location and altitude. To discuss local weather patterns, observe and consult records from the area.
messages.article.earth.summary: Discover why we have day, night, and seasons.
messages.article.earth.activity: Use a ball and a flashlight in a dark room. The ball represents Earth and the flashlight represents the Sun. Turn the ball and observe how its illuminated part changes.
messages.article.observe.title: How to start observing the sky
messages.article.observe.p1: Choose a familiar, safe location. Avoid roads, slopes, and unprotected shores. Children should go with an adult. Bring warm clothing and agree on a time to return.
messages.article.observe.p2: Choose a night with few clouds and a place with little artificial light. Let your eyes adjust to the dark. You can start with the Moon and the brightest stars without using a telescope.
messages.article.observe.p3: Record the date, time, location, and sky conditions. Draw the lights you observe. If you do not recognize an object, describe what you see before trying to name it.
messages.article.observe.p4: Visible objects change with the time, date, and location. This page does not show a live sky map. Not all lights are stars: you may also observe planets, aircraft, or artificial satellites.
messages.article.observe.p5: Comparing observations helps you learn. Keep drawings from different nights. They do not need to be perfect: they should help you remember what you saw.
messages.article.observe.summary: Plan an observation with your family or community.
messages.article.observe.activity: Download the observing guide at the bottom of the page. Complete one record and compare it with another person’s record. What did you both observe?
messages.article.glossary.title: Words for learning astronomy
messages.article.glossary.p1: Astronomy studies bodies in space and phenomena in the universe. This glossary explains words used in QAS articles.
messages.article.glossary.p2: These definitions describe scientific concepts. When translating them, a short explanation can be used if the community has no commonly used equivalent word.
messages.article.glossary.summary: Read short definitions of words used in the articles.
messages.article.glossary.activity: Choose three words. Explain each in your own words and add a drawing.
messages.glossary.star.definition: A body of hot gas that produces energy inside it. The Sun is a star.
messages.glossary.planet.definition: In the solar system, a nearly spherical body that orbits the Sun, is not a moon, and gravitationally dominates its orbital neighborhood.
messages.glossary.orbit.definition: The path of a body around another under the influence of gravity.
messages.glossary.gravity.definition: Attraction between bodies that have mass. It keeps planets in orbit around the Sun.
messages.glossary.satellite.definition: A natural body that orbits a planet or another larger body. The Moon orbits Earth.
messages.glossary.galaxy.definition: A collection of stars, gas, dust, and dark matter held together by gravity.
messages.glossary.constellation.definition: A defined region of the sky. It is often associated with an imagined pattern of stars that may be far apart from each other.
messages.glossary.lightyear.definition: The distance light travels in one year. It is a unit of distance, not time.
messages.glossary.nebula.definition: A cloud of gas and dust in space. Stars form in some nebulae.
messages.glossary.atmosphere.definition: A layer of gases surrounding a body, such as Earth.
messages.article.classroom.title: An activity for school
messages.article.classroom.p1: Starting question: why does the illuminated portion of the Moon that we see change? This activity uses a model. A model represents some features of a phenomenon but does not reproduce every detail.
messages.article.classroom.p2: Materials: a flashlight, a light-colored ball, and a space where the lights can be dimmed. The flashlight represents the Sun. The ball represents the Moon. The observer represents a viewpoint from Earth.
messages.article.classroom.p3: Keep the flashlight still. Another person slowly moves the ball around the observer. Hold the ball slightly above head level so the body does not block the light. Do not shine the flashlight into anyone’s eyes.
messages.article.classroom.p4: Observe which part of the ball receives light and how much of that illuminated part you can see. Draw three positions. Discuss the difference between the illuminated part and the visible part.
messages.article.classroom.p5: The model does not represent real distances or sizes. It also cannot explain eclipse dates by itself. Its purpose is to show how our view of an illuminated sphere changes.
messages.article.classroom.summary: Model the Moon’s phases with simple materials.
messages.article.classroom.activity: Each participant explains one drawing in their preferred language. Record any remaining questions to investigate in another session.
messages.article.stars.activity: Try this: draw two groups of stars and observe them again an hour later. Have they moved? Earth’s rotation makes them appear to move across the sky.
messages.article.planets.activity: Activity: draw the Moon over several nights and record each date. Never look directly at the Sun or view it through binoculars or telescopes without suitable solar filters.
messages.article.andes.activity: Try this together: ask a family member which words they use for the sky. With their permission, record the word, meaning, and community or language variety. Do not publish stories or recordings without permission.
